In polymorphemic complex verbs, for example, stress falls on the root-final syllable, not on the added modifier or directional (§3.1). [p. 176] There are a few disyllabic stems stressed on the first syllable which are apparently fossilised polymorphemic stems, e.g. -so'dar 'shiver, shake', -sufar 'sleep'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable and falls on the final syllable of the root (lexical nucleus); prefixes (subject/mood proclitics) and suffixes (modifiers, directionals, object markers) never attract or shift it. Within a polymorphemic complex verb the stress stays on the root-final syllable. Corroborated first-hand by the Sterners' 1987 UNCEN-SIL vocabulary ('The main stress, marked by high intonation and accent, occurs on the last syllable of the word nucleus, the part which carries the central meaning', with bi'do 'strong' / fe-bi'do-tap 'weak', yo-'siji-e 'I ask something from him').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllabic verb stems stressed on the first syllable (-so'dar 'shiver, shake', -sufar 'sleep'), explained as fossilised polymorphemic stems in which the original root is the first syllable (p.176).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: root vs. affixed word; the 2002 sketch frames it as root-final within the morphological word, the 1987 vocabulary as the last syllable of the 'word nucleus'. No phrase-level or citation-form discussion. The 2002 sketch is a compilation partly based on J. Sterner 1975, 1976, 1987 and R. Sterner 1975; the underlying primary phonology (Sterner 1975, OL 14(2)) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe Sobei proper (sobe1238) as spoken at Sarmi village, Sawar and Bagaiserwar on the Sarmi coast; no dialect distinction is made. The 2002 sketch is a compilation by Sterner & Ross partly based on the Sterners' 1975-1987 work.

sources.note: 'The main stress, marked by high intonation and accent, occurs on the last syllable of the word nucleus, the part which carries the central meaning.' Examples: bi'do 'strong', fe-bi'do-tap 'weak'; yo-'siji-e 'I ask something from him'; yo-'si'tar-e 'I question him' (stress stays on the root, prefixes and suffixes unstressed).
